chunks: Ibn Mahboub, from Umar bin Yazeed, from Bureyd al-Ajli, who said:

I asked him about a man who contracted a slave of his for one thousand dirhams, and did not stipulate upon him when he contracted him that if he was unable to pay off his contract, he would be returned to slavery. And the contracted slave paid five hundred dirhams to his master. Then the contracted slave died, leaving wealth, and left a son who was an adult.

He said: Half of whatever the contracted slave left of anything is for his master who contracted him, and the remaining half is for the son of the contracted slave, because the contracted slave died and half of him was free and half of him was a slave to the one who contracted him. So the son of the contracted slave is like his father: half of him is free and half of him is a slave.
So if he pays to the one who contracted his father whatever remained upon his father, then he is free, and there is no way for anyone of the people over him.

key_terms.رَدٌّ فِي الرِّقِّ: Reversion to slavery (if default is stipulated).
key_terms.مُكَاتَب: A slave who has entered into a contract with his master to buy his freedom for a specified sum.
key_terms.نِصْفُهُ حُرٌّ وَ نِصْفُهُ عَبْدٌ: Half-free and half-slave (status of the deceased mukatab).

ai.seo_question: What happens to the estate and freedom status of a slave who dies mid-contract for manumission?
ai.summary: This ruling from al-Kafi highlights the unique Shia jurisprudential concept of 'half-free, half-slave' status for a mukatab who dies mid-contract, distinguishing it from other schools by ensuring the estate is divided proportionally rather than fully reverting to the master. It underscores the principle of equity, allowing the son to inherit the father's partial freedom and complete the emancipation by settling the remaining debt, thereby preserving the family's dignity and economic stability.
